{{Short description|none}}
{{use dmy|date=September 2026}}
Beginning in the mid-2020s, [[Large language model|large language models]], including [[Reasoning model|reasoning models]], have made increasing progress in generating mathematical proofs at research level.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Open Proof Corpus: A Large-Scale Study of LLM-Generated Mathematical Proofs |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2506.21621v2 |access-date=2026-08-13 |website=arxiv.org |language=en |date=14 January 2026 |archive-date=13 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260813191403/https://arxiv.org/html/2506.21621v2 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Chojecki |first=Przemyslaw |date=2025-12-08 |title=Mathematics in the Age of Large Language Models |url=https://www.ulam.ai/research/deepalgebra2.pdf|website=Ulam.ai}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lee |first=Melissa |date=2026-08-09 |title=Generative AI has changed mathematics forever. Where to from here? |url=https://theconversation.com/generative-ai-has-changed-mathematics-forever-where-to-from-here-288954 |access-date=2026-08-13 |website=The Conversation |language=en-US |archive-date=14 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260814055002/https://theconversation.com/generative-ai-has-changed-mathematics-forever-where-to-from-here-288954 |url-status=live }}</ref> Most such proofs have been conducted using models from [[OpenAI]] and [[Anthropic]]. This is a list of notable discoveries conducted primarily by such models. 

The degree of human intervention in AI-generated mathematical proofs may vary and remain unclear. Subjects responsible for publishing such proofs, including individuals and AI companies such as [[OpenAI]], often fail to disclose used [[prompt engineering|prompts]], structure of pipelines used as a model workflow, or specific models used for generating proofs. The publication of such proofs may not satisfy [[Scientific method|standards of science articles]]. It may not have passed independent review or [[peer review]], and instead be published on corporate websites, personal websites, or social media.

== 2023 ==

* In December 2023, researchers at [[Google DeepMind]] used a pre-trained LLM to discover a new lower bound for the [[cap set problem]] and new algorithms for the [[bin packing problem]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Romera-Paredes |first1=Bernardino |last2=Barekatain |first2=Mohammadamin |last3=Novikov |first3=Alexander |last4=Balog |first4=Matej |last5=Kumar |first5=M. Pawan |last6=Dupont |first6=Emilien |last7=Ruiz |first7=Francisco J. R. |last8=Ellenberg |first8=Jordan S. |last9=Wang |first9=Pengming |last10=Fawzi |first10=Omar |last11=Kohli |first11=Pushmeet |last12=Fawzi |first12=Alhussein |date=14 December 2023 |title=Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models |journal=Nature |language=en |publisher=Nature Publishing Group |volume=625 |issue=7995 |pages=468–475 |doi=10.1038/s41586-023-06924-6 |pmid=38096900 |pmc=10794145 |s2cid=266223700}}</ref> The results for the cap set problem were verified by mathematician [[Jordan Ellenberg]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Paredes |first=Alhussein Fawzi and Bernardino Romera |date=2023-12-14 |title=FunSearch: Making new discoveries in mathematical sciences using Large Language Models |url=https://deepmind.google/blog/funsearch-making-new-discoveries-in-mathematical-sciences-using-large-language-models/ |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=Google DeepMind |language=en |archive-date=16 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260916090538/https://deepmind.google/blog/funsearch-making-new-discoveries-in-mathematical-sciences-using-large-language-models/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

== 2024 ==

* In October 2024, researchers at [[Meta Platforms|Meta]] and the [[Ecole des Ponts et Chaussees]] found pre-trained [[Seq2seq]] [[Transformer (deep learning)|transformers]] could discover new global [[Lyapunov function|Lyapunov functions]] at a higher rate than non-AI systems.<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 October 2024 |title=Global Lyapunov functions: a long-standing open problem in mathematics, with symbolic transformers |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2410.08304v1 |access-date=2026-09-15 |website=arxiv.org |language=en}}</ref>

== 2025 ==

* In May 2025, Google DeepMind's [[AlphaEvolve]] agent discovered an optimization for the [[Strassen algorithm]], reducing the [[Scalar multiplication|scalar multiplications]] needed for 4x4 matrices from 49 to 48. It also improved the lower bounds for 11 [[Kissing number|kissing numbers]].<ref>{{Cite web |last= |first= |date=2025-05-14 |title=AlphaEvolve: A Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms |url=https://deepmind.google/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/ |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Google DeepMind |language=en |archive-date=19 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260919100928/https://deepmind.google/blog/alphaevolve-a-gemini-powered-coding-agent-for-designing-advanced-algorithms/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In September 2025, Math Inc.'s Gauss agent formalized the strong [[prime number theorem]] in [[Lean (proof assistant)|Lean]], producing ~25,000 lines of code and formally proving >1,000 theorems.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Introducing Gauss, an agent for autoformalization |url=https://math.inc/gauss |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Math, Inc. |language=en |archive-date=10 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260910174946/https://www.math.inc/gauss |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In November 2025, researchers at Chinese universities constructed a [[reinforcement learning]] algorithm which improved the lower and upper bounds for 15 kissing numbers.<ref>{{Cite arXiv |last1=Ma |first1=Chengdong |last2=Zhaowei |first2=Théo Tao |last3=Li |first3=Pengyu |last4=Liu |first4=Minghao |last5=Chen |first5=Haojun |last6=Mao |first6=Zihao |last7=Li |first7=Bo |last8=Cheng |first8=Yuan |last9=Qi |first9=Yuan |date=2025-11-17 |title=Finding Kissing Numbers with Game-theoretic Reinforcement Learning |class=cs.LG |eprint=2511.13391v4 |language=en}}</ref>

== 2026 ==

=== Q1 ===
<!--JanuaryFebruary-->
* In February 2026, [[Google DeepMind]] used its [[Gemini (language model)|Gemini]] model to survey the 700 open [[List of conjectures by Paul Erdős|Erdős problems]], which proved four of them and found nine unknown published solutions.<ref>{{Cite web |date=5 February 2026 |title=Semi-Autonomous Mathematics Discovery with Gemini:A Case Study on the Erdős Problems |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2601.22401v3 |access-date=2026-09-12 |website=arxiv.org |archive-date=26 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260826015853/https://arxiv.org/html/2601.22401v3 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In March 2026, Math Inc.'s Gauss agent formalized [[Maryna Viazovska]]'s proofs of [[sphere packing]] in 8 and 24 dimensions, in ~200 thousand lines of Lean code.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Skuse |first=Benjamin |date=2 March 2026 |title=Watershed Moment for AI–Human Collaboration in Math > Twenty-first-century Fields Medal proof formalized for the first time |url=https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-proof-verification |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=spectrum.ieee.org |language=en |archive-date=8 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260908212134/https://spectrum.ieee.org/ai-proof-verification |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Completing the formal proof of higher-dimensional sphere packing |url=https://math.inc/sphere-packing |access-date=2026-09-14 |website=Math, Inc. |language=en |archive-date=19 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260919075112/https://www.math.inc/sphere-packing |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In March 2026, Google DeepMind's [[AlphaEvolve]] agent improved lower bounds for nine classical [[Ramsey numbers]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=10 March 2026 |title=Reinforced Generation of Combinatorial Structures: Ramsey Numbers |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2603.09172v5 |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=arxiv.org |archive-date=18 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260918013004/https://arxiv.org/html/2603.09172v5 |url-status=live }}</ref>

=== Q2 ===
<!--AprilMay-->
* In May 2026, Google DeepMind used an AlphaEvolve-like model, adapted for mathematical proofs, to prove nine Erdős problems and 44 out of 492 formalized [[On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences|OEIS]] conjectures.<ref>{{Cite web |date=21 May 2026 |title=Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2605.22763v1 |access-date=2026-09-13 |website=arxiv.org |language=en |archive-date=18 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260918230953/https://arxiv.org/html/2605.22763v1 |url-status=live }}</ref> Epoch AI then used various LLMs to prove/disprove 147 of these 492 OEIS conjectures.<ref>{{Cite web |date=13 August 2026 |title=OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems? |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2608.11941 |access-date=2026-09-13 |website=arxiv.org |archive-date=13 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260913201601/https://arxiv.org/html/2608.11941 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In May 2026, OpenAI announced an internal model produced a disproof of the [[Unit distance graph|unit distance problem]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wexler |first=Ellen |title=Mathematicians Puzzled Over a Famous Problem for 80 Years. Now, They've Used A.I. to Identify a Clever Solution |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/mathematicians-puzzled-over-a-famous-problem-for-80-years-now-theyve-used-ai-to-identify-a-clever-solution-180988889/ |access-date=2026-08-13 |website=Smithsonian Magazine |language=en |date=3 June 2026 |archive-date=14 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260814132001/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/smart-news/mathematicians-puzzled-over-a-famous-problem-for-80-years-now-theyve-used-ai-to-identify-a-clever-solution-180988889/ |url-status=live }}</ref> and several mathematicians collaborated to produce a verification and exposition of the result.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Remarks on the disproof of the unit distance conjecture |url=https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20695v1 |access-date=2026-08-13 |website=arxiv.org |date=20 May 2026 |archive-date=13 August 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260813201438/https://arxiv.org/html/2605.20695v1 |url-status=live }}</ref>
* In May 2026, Max Grinzstajn prompted [[GPT-5.5]] Pro to discover a counterexample for  [[Borsuk's conjecture]] in dimension {{Math|1=n = 63}}, the smallest dimension for which a counterexample is known.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Grinsztajn |first=Max |title=A 63-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture |url=https://github.com/maaxgrin/borsuk-63-counterexample |website=Github}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Smallest dimension in which Borsuk's conjecture fails |url=https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/28a.html |access-date=2026-09-17 |website=teorth.github.io |language=en |archive-date=18 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260918184328/https://teorth.github.io/optimizationproblems/constants/28a.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

|August 2026||unreleased version of Claude||combinatorics||[[Hadamard matrix|Hadamard matrices]] constructed for the twelve orders below 2000 for which none were previously known||Levent Alpöge, Philippe Voinov and Saul Reynolds-Haertle ||Computer-verified constructions{{Citation needed|date=September 2026}}||On 12 August, Alpöge posted constructions for Hadamard matrices for twelve unresolved orders: 668, 716, 892, 1132, 1244, 1388, 1436, 1676, 1772, 1916, 1948 and 1964. The smallest of those, 668, had been the smallest open case of the [[Hadamard conjecture]] since 2005. This improves on the original proof of the conjecture by [[Kevin Ford (mathematician)|Ford]], [[Ben J. Green|Green]], [[Sergei Konyagin|Konyagin]], [[James Maynard (mathematician)|Maynard]] and [[Terence Tao|Tao]] from 2014. ===Navier–Stokes equations===
{{details|Navier–Stokes priority controversy}}
In September 2026, OpenAI claimed an internal model more powerful than [[GPT-6 Astra]] had solved the [[Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness]] problem, one of the [[Millennium Prize Problems]]. The claim has not been verified by the wider mathematical community. The credit for the discovery is disputed.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Howlett |first=Joseph |title=OpenAI claims blockbuster math breakthrough amid swirl of controversy |url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-claims-blockbuster-math-breakthrough-amid-swirl-of-controversy/ |access-date=2026-09-09 |website=Scientific American |language=en |date=8 September 2026 |archive-date=8 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260908230102/https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/openai-claims-blockbuster-math-breakthrough-amid-swirl-of-controversy/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite magazine |last1=Knight |first1=Will |last2=Zeff |first2=Maxwell |date=2026-09-08 |title=OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul |url=https://www.wired.com/story/openai-navier-stokes-math-discovery-academics/ |access-date=2026-09-09 |magazine=Wired |language=en-US |issn=1059-1028 |archive-date=9 September 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260909002647/https://www.wired.com/story/openai-navier-stokes-math-discovery-academics/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
